title: Febrile seizures (India, IAP)
subject: paediatrics
setting: Home, emergency department, paediatric ward and outpatients
summary: Febrile seizures occur with fever in children aged 6 months to 6 years without CNS infection. Stop an ongoing seizure with intranasal midazolam, look for the fever source and red flags, investigate simple seizures minimally, and reserve intermittent clobazam or continuous prophylaxis for selected children; antipyretics do not prevent recurrence.

sections.title: Definitions
items: Febrile seizure: seizure with fever in a child aged 6 months to 6 years, without CNS infection, metabolic or electrolyte disturbance, previous afebrile seizure, or acute neurological insult. Most occur within 24 hours of fever onset.
Simple: isolated generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting under 15 minutes that does not recur within 24 hours.
Complex: focal, longer than 15 minutes, recurring within 24 hours, or incomplete recovery within 1 hour.
Febrile status epilepticus: seizure lasting 30 minutes or more, or a series without full recovery in between.
Febrile seizures plus: continuing beyond 6 years and/or with afebrile seizures; with a family history this suggests genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+).

sections.title: If the child is still seizing
items: Stabilise with an ABCDE approach (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure).
Home or first rescue: intranasal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (maximum 5 mg). Alternatives: IM or buccal midazolam, buccal lorazepam, or rectal diazepam. Maximum 2 doses, 5 minutes apart.
In hospital, manage febrile status epilepticus as convulsive status epilepticus.
Avoid sodium channel blockers (phenytoin) if Dravet syndrome or GEFS+ is known.
If meningitis is suspected in a young child with febrile status, start a third-generation cephalosporin until CSF results are available.

sections.title: Evaluation after a first febrile seizure
items: History: seizure type and duration, postictal phase, fever source (ear discharge, dysuria), antibiotics or antipyretics already given, immunisation (Hib, pneumococcal), previous seizures, development, and family history of febrile seizures or epilepsy.

Red flags: meningeal signs or bulging fontanelle, focal neurological signs, altered sensorium persisting 1 hour after the seizure, raised intracranial pressure, non-blanching rash in an unwell child, sepsis, shock or respiratory distress.

Simple seizure: no routine EEG, imaging or blood tests. Lumbar puncture if meningitis is suspected, and consider it under 12 months if Hib or pneumococcal vaccines are missing, after antibiotic pretreatment, or with severe malnutrition. Serum calcium if under 1 year.

Complex seizure or febrile status: CBC with CRP, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium and glucose; consider lumbar puncture if still obtunded 1 hour after the seizure; EEG after 48 hours and within 1 week; MRI (preferably within 72 hours) for suspected encephalitis, ADEM, a mass, malformation, or pre-existing developmental delay.
Image before lumbar puncture if there are focal deficits or signs of raised intracranial pressure. Urine analysis under 18 months or with urinary symptoms; serum iron if pale.
Genetic testing for Dravet syndrome (SCN1A and related genes) for recurrent febrile status, prolonged hemiconvulsive seizures under 1 year, vaccine-associated encephalopathy, or GEFS+.

sections.title: Fever and prophylaxis
items: Treat the cause of fever. Paracetamol 15 mg/kg per dose as needed, up to 6-hourly, and tepid sponging improve comfort but do not prevent febrile seizures.
No continuous or intermittent anticonvulsants after one or more simple febrile seizures: harm outweighs benefit.

Intermittent prophylaxis may be considered for frequent recurrent simple seizures with high parental anxiety or distance from care, or complex seizures not on continuous therapy: clobazam 0.5 to 1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 3 days during fever, without tapering (maximum 20 mg/day).

Continuous prophylaxis may be considered for febrile status epilepticus, febrile seizures with neurodevelopmental disorders (cerebral palsy, global delay, autism), frequent complex seizures, or febrile seizures plus or GEFS+ with afebrile seizures: sodium valproate 20 to 40 mg/kg/day (first choice), or phenobarbital 3 to 5 mg/kg/day, or primidone 15 to 20 mg/kg/day, usually for 2 seizure-free years. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are ineffective.

Valproate carries rare fatal hepatotoxicity, highest under 2 years; phenobarbital causes behaviour and sleep problems; intermittent benzodiazepines cause drowsiness and ataxia and may mask CNS infection.

sections.title: Counselling and prognosis
items: Reassure parents: simple febrile seizures do not damage the brain or affect learning, and the risk of death is negligible.

About 32% have a recurrence. Risk factors: first seizure under 18 months, family history of febrile seizures or epilepsy, seizure with fever below 39°C, fever for less than 1 hour before the seizure, complex seizure, day-care attendance.
Epilepsy risk after simple febrile seizures is about 1% by 7 years (similar to the general population). After complex seizures: about 6 to 8% with 1 complex feature, 17 to 22% with 2, and 49% with 3.
Teach first aid (side position, nothing in the mouth, time the seizure) and how to give intranasal midazolam for a seizure that has not stopped; seek care after any rescue dose.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Missing meningitis in an infant who is unimmunised, pretreated with antibiotics or not recovering within 1 hour.
Routine EEG, CT or blood tests after a simple febrile seizure.
Starting long-term anticonvulsants after a simple febrile seizure.
Telling parents that regular antipyretics will prevent the next seizure.
Using phenytoin in suspected Dravet syndrome.

drugs.name: Midazolam (intranasal)
drugs.dose: 0.2 mg/kg, maximum 5 mg; may repeat once after 5 minutes (maximum 2 doses)
drugs.notes: First choice rescue at home; IM or buccal routes also effective.

drugs.name: Clobazam (intermittent prophylaxis)
drugs.dose: 0.5 to 1 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses for 3 days of fever, maximum 20 mg/day
drugs.notes: No taper needed. Selected children only.

drugs.name: Sodium valproate (continuous prophylaxis)
drugs.notes: Rare fatal hepatotoxicity, highest under 2 years; thrombocytopenia, pancreatitis.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg per dose as needed, up to 6-hourly
drugs.notes: Comfort only; does not prevent seizures.
